4863.prule: One stressed vowel per word whose position is a lexical property of the word (morpheme-inherent), not computable from syllable count or weight. Hymes 1984 states no placement rule; she presupposes one lexically stressed vowel per word and reports that Warm Springs has lost the historically stressed vowel of many words, the stress moving to the remaining vowel, so Warm Springs stress positions differ lexically from those of the other Sahaptin dialects (pt'x̣ánu vs. pə́t'x̣anu; twít'aš vs. túwit'aš; ápx vs. əpə́x; núkʷt vs. nəkʷə́t). General Sahaptin statement (Umatilla/Columbia River data with some Warm Springs forms): Rude 2006:272 'Though there are patterns, stress is morpheme inherent in Sahaptin in so far as there is no universally applicable principle such as the penultimate stress rule in Nez Perce'; Rude 2012:302 'In Sahaptin all lexical morphemes have morpheme inherent stress.'

In the latter group, ordinary words have only one syllable accented and no secondary stress ... Short vowels have high tone; long vowels or diphthongs in accented syllables have falling tone, high to normal.

4865.dloc: Apéndice A 'Fonología y ortografía', sec. 8 'Raíces', p. 779; companion statements sec. 5 p. 777 and sec. 7 p. 778.
4865.heavy: Not weight-conditioned. Vowel length is a consequence of accent, not a condition: 'En las raíces monosílabas, además de llevar el acento prosódico, la vocal se alarga más o menos al doble' (p. 779); 'En las raíces bisílabas, las dos vocales son cortas a menos que se añada un tono por su posición sintáctica' (p. 779); the same page says either accent or length could be written since each determines the other ('el acento prosódico (que determinaría entonces la duración de vocales) o la duración de vocales (que determinaría el acento prosódico)').
4865.prule: Root-initial, non-contrastive: a 'very light' prosodic accent falls on the first syllable of the root (roots are 1-2 syllables) and stays there when prefixes are added; the monosyllabic 'determinants' (verb prefixes, bound/relative pronouns, demonstratives, some adverbs and particles) are never accented. Position within the word therefore follows morphological structure, not syllable count: cu³ndú¹ 'voy a cardar' (root -u³ndu¹, determinant c-) is accented on the penult, cu⁴ndú²¹ 'voy a montar' (root ndu²¹, determinant cu⁴-) on the final syllable, whose vowel is also lengthened (monosyllabic roots lengthen their vowel about twofold; disyllabic roots keep short vowels unless a tone glide is added syntactically). Accent and vowel length are predictable and left unwritten in the orthography.
4865.srule: Not mentioned in Anderson & Concepción Roque 1983, Apéndice A 'Fonología y ortografía' secs 5, 7, 8 (pp. 777-779; whole appendix pp. 773-794): a single 'very light' root-initial accent is described and no secondary, rhythmic or compound accent. 4865.tone: Tonal language: four contrasting tone levels (1 high - 4 low) plus glides in the Santa María Pápalo dialect ('el contraste de los cuatro niveles diferentes', p. 780); Needham & Davis 1946 give three registers (high, mid, low) for Concepción Pápalo. Both sources call stress non-phonemic ('acento prosódico... fáciles de predecir'; 'Stress is not phonemic'); tone is the lexically contrastive prosody, accent is a predictable root-initial prominence, and monosyllabic accented roots lengthen their vowel. Spanish loans receive fixed tone melodies keyed to the Spanish stress position (sec. 18).

tn.quote: Una de las caracteristicas mas notables del cuicateco es la presencia de tonos en las vocales. El tono ... sirve para dar diferentes significados a las palabras. ... El dialecto de Santa Marla Papalo tiene cuatro diferentes niveles de tono. El tono alto se representa con el numero 1, el tono bajo con el numero 4, y los tonos intermedios con los numeros 2 y 3. ... Los tonos largos de nivel 1, 2, 3 o 4 y los deslizamientos de tonos 14, 24, 243, 32 o 43 aparecen en las raices monosilabas
tn.translation: One of the most notable characteristics of Cuicateco is the presence of tones on the vowels. Tone ... serves to give different meanings to words. ... 4870.prule: No stress rule. Kalenjin (Terik included in Rottland's own corpus as dialect unit 10) is a tone language; Rottland finds no stress in phonemic function in his recordings and does not mark it; phonetically prominent ('betonte') syllables are perceptible but always coincide with a non-low (high or falling) tone, i.e. prominence is parasitic on tone, not independently placed. Terik-specific first-hand prosody (Creider 1981: 29) is tone only: Terik preserves the three-way H / L / HF contrast.

4870.tone: Rottland 1982 sec. 5.1.3.3 (pp. 78-79): Tucker (1964: 457) gives three simple tones (Hoch, Mittel, Tief) for the Kalenjin languages plus glides -- a falling tone and three position-conditioned rising tones (Hoch-Tief, Hoch-Mittel, Mittel-Hoch) -- and marks downstep ('die Herabsetzung der hohen Ebene'); Montgomery (1966: 38) posits three simple tonemes plus three glide tonemes (Mittel-Hoch, Tief-Mittel, Mittel-Tief) for Sapiny. Rottland's own position in the opened excerpt is a rejection of a phonemic mid level: 'Ich habe dieses Beispiel mit meinen Sapiny-Informanten geprüft und keinen Unterschied zwischen einer mittelhohen und einer hohen finalen Silbe gehört. Auch sonst habe ich im Kalenjin kein Indiz für eine mittlere phonemische Tonebene gefunden.' On stress (sec. 5.1.3.2): Tucker/Bryan's 'stressed syllables' are said to correlate with high or rising tone and only pitch is marked by them; in Heine's (1973) Sogoo vocabulary stress is marked independently of pitch, goes with high or falling tone, and is otherwise unpredictable; Rottland finds no phonemic stress in his own recordings and marks none; phonetically stressed syllables are recognisable and always bear non-low tone. Creider 1981: 29 (first-hand, Terik): the earlier three-way tonal contrast (high, low, high falling) is preserved; High Fall Lowering was borrowed from Nandi, Final Fall was not (te:tá 'cow', cf. Nandi te:tà).

tn.quote: Terik speakers appear to have migrated from the Mt. Elgon area prior to the merger of high and high falling tones, since they preserve the earlier three-way tonal contrast. They have borrowed the rule of High Fall Lowering from Nandi (rò:t-wa 'knife'), but not Final Fall (te:tá 'cow', cf. Nandi te:tà). High Fall Creation and High Fall Raising are present (no:ŋê:t 'shield', ó:rê:t 'road'), but it is not possible to tell if these are borrowings or retentions. The Mt. Elgon rule of High Spreading is found in Terik, but it is restricted to primary suffixes (tín-yá 'kindred', cf. Nandi tíl-yá).

4871.prule: Lexical, contrastive word stress: every word of two or more syllables has one stressed syllable, which may fall on any of the last three syllables (right-edge three-syllable window); minimal pairs /ˈkasa/ 'house' vs /kaˈsa/ 'to marry', /ˈduda/ 'doubt' vs /duˈda/ 'to doubt'. Basic-vocabulary count (monosyllables excluded): penult 61.6%, final 37.7%, antepenult 0.6%. Verbs typically final-stressed (four listed exceptions), but final stress is not confined to verbs (many Spanish- and Tagalog-origin nouns). In most words stress reproduces the primary stress of the Spanish or Tagalog etymon. No fixed-position or weight-based rule is stated; placement is not predictable from phonological shape.
4871.srule: Only in compounds and reduplications: compounds normally stress the second word, but occasionally the first word takes primary and the second word secondary stress ([ˌbuskaˈbida] ~ [ˈbuskaˌbida] 'work', [gumiˌtakaˈga] ~ [gumiˈtakaˌga]); reduplications may show [ˌkosaˈkosa] beside [kosaˈkosa] / [ˈkosaˈkosa]. tn.quote: Pareciera no existir un único parámetro acústico de la prominencia, siendo tres los que intervienen en la sílaba tónica: altura tonal en la forma de la altura de la vocal; intensidad en la forma de la energía muscular con que se expulsa el aire durante la articulación de la vocal: y la duración relativa de la vocal acentuada … El acento es distintivo a nivel semántico … La entonación tiene funciones gramaticales y pragmáticas en el CT. … podemos identificar tres tipos básicos finales: descendente, ascendente y suspensión.
tn.translation: There seems to be no single acoustic parameter of prominence; three are involved in the stressed syllable: pitch height, in the form of the height of the vowel; intensity, in the form of the muscular energy with which air is expelled during the articulation of the vowel; and the relative duration of the stressed vowel … Stress is semantically distinctive … Intonation has grammatical and pragmatic functions in Ternate Chabacano. … we can identify three basic final [intonation] types: falling, rising and suspended.

4877.prule: No word-stress rule is stated. The source describes a morpheme-level pitch/register system: pitch register (high vs low) is conditioned by vowel quality (clear = high, breathy = low), and within each register there is a phonemic contrast between level and contour pitch (breathy: low level vs low-rising-falling; clear: high level vs extra-high-falling), giving the four word-base classes also reported by Pittman 1970; the contrast is a property of the morpheme, not the syllable. 'Stress' is used only for intonational stress (pitch upstep plus intensity) assigned by utterance intonation patterns (heavy stress on the utterance-final syllable before the ') ' and '!' marks, on the first syllable of a question word, lighter stress on the question morpheme, 'some stress' before a comma).

4882.srule: Not mentioned in Koch 2008 (secs. 3.3.8, 4.2, 5.2.7, 8.4.1 read; Koch separates only word-level stress from phrasal/nuclear stress). dfl.q: To summarize the TRS stress pattern, when a word has only one stressable morpheme (i.e. the root), primary stress falls on the root (ex.1); when a word has multiple stressable morphemes, but all of them are unaccented, primary stress falls on the first stressable suffix (ex. 2a, 3a, 4a). When a word has one or more accented morphemes, stress falls on the rightmost accented morpheme (ex. 5, 6).

deciding.quote: Generalizing across Mixtec varieties, Josserand (1983:180) defines the couplet as “composed of two syllables and carrying stress on the first of these two,” implying that all Mixtec varieties have the same stress behavior. Besides the data from Santo Domingo Nuxaa shown in (4.2), several other descriptions support the characterization of stress in Mixtec as falling on the first vowel of the couplet. ... In sum, default stress on the first syllable of the couplet is widely reported in Mixtec.

tn.note: Tone of Tidaá Mixtec is undescribed in any obtainable source; the sole work with Tidaá data (Josserand 1983, a dialect-survey wordlist) is license-gated. Mixtec languages generally are tonal.

4886.cfw: Nothing describes Tidaá stress itself: the only work with Tidaá data is Josserand's 1983 comparative survey, whose family-wide statement that the Mixtec couplet carries stress on its first syllable is known only as quoted by Carroll 2015 and Penner 2019, so any placement for Tidaá is an inference from the family, not a finding.

tn.translation: Kɪtíínɪ́ has two basic tones: high and low, represented here respectively by the acute accent and, generally, by the absence of any diacritic for reasons of economy. Vowel contraction (3.1.) allows the generation of complex tones (rising and falling). A few roots have however been optionally noted with a falling tone. ... Value of the tones. The tones have both a lexical and a grammatical value.

tn.note: Two basic tones, H and L (L unmarked); rising and falling arise from vowel contraction (L+H, H+L), a few roots optionally noted falling. Tone is lexical and grammatical. Nothing on stress.

4889.dq: In non-inflected words of two or three syllables in which all vowels are short and in which the final syllable is closed by a consonant, primary stress occurs on the final syllable. ... The above rules apply to the stems of inflected words. (Boush & Boush 1974 treat clause-level pitch separately under 3.3.2 'Intonation'.)
4889.dloc: Steinkraus 1969 sec. 7 'Stress', p. 64; sec. 6 'Tonemes', pp. 63-64. Boush & Boush 1974 sec. 3.3.1, pp. 25-27.
4889.heavy: a syllable 'with a lengthened vowel' (long vowel); when no vowel in the word is long, a final syllable 'closed by a consonant' takes the stress (closed non-final syllables do not attract it: /amdu/ ['amdu] 'mountain', /kaltabni/ ['kaltabni] 'your own', Boush & Boush p. 26)
4889.dflt: final syllable if closed by a consonant, initial syllable if the final syllable is open (stated for non-inflected words of 2-3 syllables and for the stems of inflected words; not posited for the rare all-short non-inflected words of more than three syllables)
4889.prule: Primary stress falls on the first (leftmost) syllable containing a lengthened (long) vowel, wherever it is in the word. If every vowel is short (stated for non-inflected words of two or three syllables), stress is final when the final syllable is closed by a consonant and initial when the final syllable is open; the same rules apply to the stems of inflected words (Boush & Boush 1974 p. 26: 'primary stress on inflected words occur on the final syllable of a simple verb stem').
4889.srule: Secondary stress on the second syllable with a long (lengthened) vowel; in inflected words of more than three syllables with all vowels short, on the antepenult; none in words of three or fewer syllables with all vowels short (Steinkraus 1969 p. 64, Okbiilabib dialect). Boush & Boush 1974 p. 26 (Balemtilabib dialect): in inflected words of four or more syllables, secondary stress on the final (suffix) syllable.
4889.quote: Primary stress is predictable by the following rules: Primary stress occurs on the first syllable with a lengthened vowel. In non-inflected words of two or three syllables in which all vowels are short and in which the final syllable is closed by a consonant, primary stress occurs on the final syllable. In non-inflected words of two or three syllables in which all vowels are short and in which the final syllable is open, primary stress occurs on the initial syllable. The above rules apply to the stems of inflected words. Non-inflected words of more than three syllables in which all vowels are…

4889.idn: Tifal, a member of the Mountain-Ok sub-family; Steinkraus's data are from the village of Okbiilabib in the Ilam river valley. (Boush & Boush 1974 describe the speech of Balemtilabib, Lam River valley, and call Steinkraus's data 'a closely related dialect'.); data: Okbiilabib village, Ilam…
4889.exq_: Non-inflected words of more than three syllables in which all vowels are short are extremely rare, and stress rules have not yet been posited for them. (Steinkraus 1969 p. 64.) Boush & Boush 1974 p. 27: 'stress rules for complex or compound verbs have not been posited at this time.'
4889.tone: Steinkraus 1969 sec. 6 p. 63: 'Tifal has a two toneme system with contrast between high and low tones. High tone is marked with an acute accent and low tone with a grave accent. The pitch range between high and low is quite narrow.'... 'Only one toneme occurs per syllable, whether the nucleus consists of a short or long vowel.' P. 64: 'Any word initial syllable with a short vowel nucleus has neutralized tone on that syllable.' Stress is described separately (sec. 7) as fully predictable, so tone and stress coexist in his analysis. Boush & Boush 1974 fn. 3 p. 25 (Balemtilabib/Lam-valley dialect, via saved scan): 'Thus far, tone has been found to be non-contrastive. This differs from the work done in a related dialect by Walter Steinkraus, TIFAL TONE. Stress seems to be more crucial.' The 2004 OPD (data checked by Boush 1994) states only the predictable stress rule and no tone. The disagreement is about tone, not about stress placement, on which all three sources give the same rule; hence weight-sensitive with a fixed default with the tonal analysis flagged rather than as tone/pitch accent or as a source conflict.

tn.quote: Tifal has a two toneme system with contrast between high and low tones. High tone is marked with an acute accent and low tone with a grave accent. The pitch range between high and low is quite narrow. A particular pitch is relative to others in its environment so that a toneme of a mono-toneme cannot be distinguished in isolation. Only one toneme occurs per syllable, whether the nucleus consists of a short or long vowel. Contrast can be shown on monosyllabic words as follows. … Any word initial syllable with a short vowel nucleus has neutralized tone on that syllable.
tn.cite: Steinkraus, Walter. 1969. Tifal phonology showing vowel and tone neutralization. Kivung 2(1): 57-66.
tn.note: Two level tonemes, high and low, one per syllable (long or short vowel); tone neutralized on word-initial short-vowel syllables; separate word stress, predictable from vowel length and syllable shape.
